title: Hildegard's music
hookLine: the abbess wrote a whole cycle of chants, some still sung
carry: feather on the breath of god

cards: Nuns are singing in a stone church above the Rhine, and the melody does something strange. It leaps. It climbs high, swoops low, and hangs on a single syllable for a long breath before it lets go.
The woman who wrote it is their abbess, Hildegard of Bingen. She wrote books of visions, letters to popes and emperors, and works on medicine and the natural world.
And she wrote songs for her community to sing, gathered under the name Symphonia. Choirs still sing some of them.

teach.h: A FEATHER ON THE BREATH OF GOD.
teach.b: Hildegard didn't describe her gift as cleverness. In a letter she told a story about herself. In paraphrase: a king once lifted a small feather from the ground and told it to fly.
It flew, not because of anything in the feather, but because the air carried it. That, she said, was her: a feather on the breath of God. Not a boast.
A confession that she was carried. Music mattered enough to her that she fought for it.

teach.h: THE NUNS ARE FORBIDDEN TO SING.
teach.b: Once, church authorities placed her community under a ban, and her nuns were forbidden to sing the office aloud.
Hildegard wrote to the prelates of Mainz in protest. In paraphrase: before the fall, Adam's voice joined the angels in praise. The prophets made psalms and instruments to stir hearts toward God.
And those who silence singing in church without good reason should take care. Her ground was the psalms.
Psalm 150, in the King James words, calls for trumpet and harp, timbrel and dance, "stringed instruments and organs," and then turns to everything that has breath, and calls it to praise.
Set the feather beside the psalm, and breath is the link. The air carries the feather. Breath carries the song.
Christians use music in prayer in very different ways, from silent meetings to plain hymns to full choirs, and each church has its reasons. Hildegard's way is one of them: wide, soaring, and sung.

how: Some monasteries and choirs still sing Hildegard's chants in worship and concerts, and Catholics honor her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

games.q: you're Hildegard. church authorities have forbidden your nuns to sing the office aloud. what do you do?
o: obey in silence and say nothing.
write to the prelates, defending sung praise.
games.why: she wrote to the prelates of Mainz: the prophets made psalms and instruments to stir hearts toward God, and those who silence singing without good reason should take care.

practice: Play a recording of medieval chant, one of Hildegard's if you can find one, and simply listen; if you can't, sit in silence and listen to your own breath.

Let the week drift past as well: Cluny's long prayer, the slow break of ten fifty-four, Anselm's question, the crusades told honestly, Bernard's plain walls, and now this music, and let one of them stay with you.
If you pray, let the music be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Hildegard's music. The soaring chants an abbess on the Rhine wrote for her nuns, made, as she understood it, by a feather on the breath of God.

orig.note: Latin: harmony — the name by which Hildegard's collection of songs is known.
